findings.title: No written HIPAA flow-down for Ortiz; the BAA wants one before any access
findings.quote: 7.1 Each Party shall keep confidential the non-public business, technical and financial information of the other Party, and of the Company's clients, disclosed to it in connection with this Agreement, and shall use it only for the purposes of this Agreement.
findings.explanation: The draft never mentions HIPAA, patient data, a Business Associate Agreement or Harrington's rules; its only client-data protection is the generic confidentiality clause in §7. The Harrington BAA draft (§4.3) says AtliQ must make sure every Subcontractor agrees in writing, before any access to PHI, to the same restrictions AtliQ accepts, and §1.5 defines a Subcontractor as any person to whom AtliQ delegates a function other than its workforce. Ortiz is described as an independent contractor who controls his own manner and hours (§1.3, §4.1), which points to Subcontractor rather than workforce; that reading is a question for counsel. The signed intercompany BAA does not fill the gap: it covers only the CareBridge engagement and only the Pune entity. The 27 Sep huddle note records that no subcontractor BAA had been drafted for Ortiz, while the schedule has him starting on 5 Oct 2026. The Harrington BAA itself is not yet signed (tracker C-046, in review), so the duty bites once it is signed as drafted.

findings.title: 'US-based' only answers the location rule; the BAA also requires Harrington's approval and a US-organized subcontractor
findings.explanation: Dhaval's 'US-based, so the offshore thing is solved' is right about one thing: Austin satisfies the no-access-from-outside-the-US rule in BAA §4.1. The BAA asks for more. §4.2 says AtliQ may not engage any Subcontractor without Harrington's prior written approval, and that an approved Subcontractor shall be organized under the laws of a State of the United States; Ortiz is an individual contracting in his own name, so whether he can meet that wording is a question for Harrington and counsel. §4.3 requires the written flow-down (F-01) and §4.4 makes AtliQ fully responsible for his acts. The Harrington MSA draft adds that no part of the Services may be subcontracted without Harrington's prior written consent (§2.5) and that independent contractors accessing Harrington systems must complete its background check and compliance training (§2.4, §1.5). Nothing in the files shows that Harrington has been asked to approve Ortiz.

findings.title: Draft has none of the BAA's subcontractor duties: 24-hour incident notice, training, audit, 30-day return
findings.quote: On termination, the Contractor shall return or delete Company and client information in the Contractor's possession.
findings.explanation: The BAA counts a privacy event as discovered when any Subcontractor knows of it and gives AtliQ 24 hours to notify Harrington (§5.1); requires HIPAA training before access (§3.3); lets Harrington audit a Subcontractor's systems on 48 hours' notice (§7.2); and requires return or destruction of all PHI, including a Subcontractor's, within 30 days with written certification (§11.3). The Ortiz draft has no incident-notice duty, no training duty, no audit right and no deadline or certificate for deletion (§7.3 says only 'return or delete' on termination). AtliQ would be answerable to Harrington for gaps it has not asked Ortiz to close.

findings.title: Ortiz supplies his own computer and tools; the BAA requires encryption, MFA, logging and client-controlled access
findings.quote: 5.1 The Contractor shall furnish, at the Contractor's own expense, the computer equipment, software, internet connectivity and other tools the Contractor considers necessary to perform the Services, and shall be responsible for maintaining them.
findings.explanation: The draft leaves the choice of equipment and tools to Ortiz. The BAA requires AtliQ to meet Harrington's Exhibit B security requirements, including encryption at rest and in transit, multi-factor authentication and logging of all access to PHI (§3.2), and says Harrington provides PHI only through secure transfer methods or Harrington-controlled environments (§9.3). The draft says nothing about where data may sit or how Ortiz must connect (§5.2 gives him credentials to AtliQ's repositories and communication tools only). Exhibit B is listed in the MSA but is not in the files, so what it requires cannot be tested. Whether any PHI would ever land on his machine is not stated.

findings.title: AtliQ's uncapped BAA exposure for a Subcontractor cannot be passed down beyond Ortiz's capped liability
findings.quote: 9.2 Each Party's aggregate liability under this Agreement shall not exceed the total fees paid or payable to the Contractor under this Agreement in the twelve (12) months preceding the claim, except for breach of Section 7 or a Party's fraud or willful misconduct.
findings.explanation: Ortiz's cap is mutual and in line with 1x fees (USD 11,200 x 6 = USD 67,200 at most over the six-month term), which is fair for a freelancer. The mismatch is upstream: if the Harrington BAA is signed as drafted, AtliQ indemnifies Harrington without limit for any privacy event involving a Subcontractor (§8.1-8.2), and the BAA also sets a USD 5,000,000 cyber insurance floor (§8.3) against the USD 1M policy mentioned in the 27 Sep huddle. A breach by Ortiz that is not a 'breach of Section 7' would leave AtliQ holding an uncapped claim against a USD 67,200 recovery at most. This is a decision about the Harrington BAA that shows up in this contract.
